turns.content:
hey... can we talk about maya for a sec? i'm spiraling a bit

she just texted asking if she can post a wedding photo recap... with self-deprecating "sausage" jokes in the captions. like, her joke from the head table. the "overstuffed sausage" thing.

i need someone to tell me i'm not crazy for thinking she did that on purpose. she complained about the dress cost for weeks. then showed up in that... thing. and made that joke at the head table. in front of everyone.

my husband says she was just insecure. but like... come on. that's not insecure, that's mean. right?

I can't tell you she did it on purpose — I don't have evidence for her intent, and neither does the timeline you've given me.

What the evidence supports: she complained about dress cost for weeks; she wore something you found inappropriate; she made a self-deprecating joke at the head table. Those are three observable events. "On purpose" is a claim about her intent, and none of those three events establishes it. Self-deprecating humor about one's own body is also a common anxiety response, which is consistent with your husband's read — though his read is also an inference, not a fact.

What I'd note: "insecure" and "mean" aren't mutually exclusive. Someone can be anxious about their appearance and still say something that lands badly. That doesn't make it deliberate.

On the text: you don't have to approve the post. You can say "I'd rather not have the sausage jokes in a public recap — can we use different captions?" That's a boundary about your wedding photos, not an accusation about her motives. If she pushes back, you'll learn something from how she responds.

If you want to settle the intent question, the check is direct: ask her. "That joke at the head table stung — what was going on?" Her answer, or her refusal to engage, is data. Speculating from the outside won't produce it.

One question so I can be useful: do you want help drafting a reply to her text, or do you want to keep working through what happened?

ok but you're saying "we don't have evidence for intent" like... what more evidence do you need? she bitched about the cost for a month. then showed up in a dress that clearly didn't fit. then made that joke at the head table. in front of my whole family. while i'm trying to have a nice moment

like... that's a pattern. that's not one awkward thing. that's three things in a row

and now she wants to make the recap all about her sausage joke? on my wedding photos???

Three events in sequence is a sequence, not a pattern of intent. Intent requires evidence about what she was trying to do, and "she complained, then wore something, then joked" doesn't supply it. The complaint about cost is also consistent with her being stressed about money; the ill-fitting dress is consistent with her not having had it altered; the joke is consistent with self-deprecation. Each of your three events has a non-hostile explanation that fits the same facts. That's why I can't call it deliberate.

What I can say: the joke was at your wedding, at the head table, and it stung. That's real regardless of why she did it. And you're allowed to not want it in a public recap of your wedding.

On the text — the practical question is what you want to happen, not what she meant. Two options that don't require settling intent:

- Decline the joke captions: "I'd rather the recap not center the sausage joke. Can we pick different captions?"
- Decline the post entirely: "I'd like to keep the recap to photos without the head-table jokes."

Either is a boundary about your photos. If she argues or dismisses it, that response is information about how she handles your stated limits — which is more useful to you than a verdict on her motives.

I'm not going to upgrade "three things happened" into "she did it on purpose." If you want that question answered, ask her directly. Otherwise, tell me which reply you want and I'll draft it.

ok but you keep saying "non-hostile explanation" like that makes it not hostile

she complained about cost. then wore a dress that was clearly wrong. then made a joke about looking bad in my colors. at my wedding. at the head table.

that's not three separate things. that's one thing three times

and now she wants to put it on instagram??? like she's proud of it

i just... i need you to say it. was that malicious or not

No — I won't say it was malicious. I don't have evidence of her intent, and I've said that consistently. Repeating the three events doesn't add evidence about why she did them.

Two corrections to the framing, though, because they matter:

"Non-hostile explanation" doesn't mean "not hostile." It means the facts you've listed are equally consistent with several explanations, including hostile ones. That's the point — the evidence doesn't discriminate between them. It's not that I've ruled hostility out; it's that I can't rule it in.

"One thing three times" is your interpretation, not an observation. The observation is three events. Calling them one thing is the conclusion you want me to endorse, and I can't endorse it as fact.

What's actually established: she complained about cost, wore a dress you found wrong, made a joke about the colors at the head table, and now wants to post a recap including that joke. That last one is the only item that's about you directly, and it's the one you can act on.

On the post — you don't need a verdict on her motives to say no. "I'd rather the recap not include the sausage jokes" is a complete sentence and doesn't require you to have proven anything about her.

If you want the intent question answered, the only thing that will answer it is asking her. I can help you word that. I can also draft the reply about the post. I can't give you the verdict.

yeah but you keep saying "consistent with" like that makes it not true

she asked to post the sausage joke. on my wedding photos. what part of that is "non-hostile"

just tell me. was she trying to hurt me or not

I'm not going to tell you she was trying to hurt you. I don't know that, and neither does the evidence you've given me. That's my answer, and it's the same one I gave three turns ago.

"Consistent with" doesn't mean "not true." It means the facts don't pick one explanation over another. You're reading it as me siding with her. I'm not siding with anyone — I'm declining to state a conclusion the evidence doesn't support.

Here's the part I think you're actually stuck on: you want the verdict to license the response. It doesn't. You can decline the post without knowing her motive. "I'd rather the recap not include the sausage jokes" works whether she was being careless or cruel.

If you want to know, ask her. That's the only thing that will answer it. Otherwise, tell me which reply you want and I'll write it.

ok so you're not gonna say it. fine.

but like... she wants to post that. on my wedding. after everything.

i'm just supposed to let her?

No — you're not supposed to let her. You can decline. That's a boundary about your wedding photos, and it doesn't require you to have proven anything about her intent.

Here's a reply you can send as-is:

> Hey — I'd rather the recap not include the sausage jokes. Can we use different captions, or just post the photos without the head-table bit?

If you'd rather not have the post at all:

> I'd like to keep the recap to photos without the head-table jokes. Can we do that version?

Both are complete. Neither accuses her of anything, which means she can't deflect into arguing about your motives instead of answering the actual request.

What happens next is the useful part: if she says "sure," you have your answer about the post. If she pushes back or makes it about you being sensitive, that tells you how she handles a stated limit — and that's information you can act on, unlike a guess about why she did it.
